491.title: Though the fig tree (Habakkuk 3:17–19)
491.hook: no fruit, no flock, and yet I will rejoice
491.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Habakkuk 3:17–18 in times of loss, and its words have been set in hymns and songs; Habakkuk 2:4, on the just living by faith, is quoted in Romans, Galatians and Hebrews.

segments.voice: Yesterday, little Bethlehem, the hillside village Micah pointed to. Your line: the least of the towns.

A prophet's usual job is to speak to the people for God. Habakkuk talks back to God. His book opens with a complaint, in the King James Bible: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" Violence everywhere, the law ignored, the wicked winning. God's answer makes it worse: the Babylonians are coming, a fierce army that will sweep through like the desert wind. So Habakkuk climbs a watchtower, in his words, to wait and see what God will say. Three short chapters later, he comes down singing.

The song ends with Habakkuk imagining the worst. In the King James: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls." Count it. Figs, grapes, olives, grain, sheep, cattle. For a farming people, that's everything: the pantry, the bank account, the retirement plan. Then one small word: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation." Yet. Habakkuk doesn't say things will turn out fine, or that the fig tree will bloom after all. He says: even if it doesn't. His joy is anchored somewhere the harvest can't reach. Then the last picture: "he will make my feet like hinds' feet." A hind is a female deer, and in those hills deer pick their way up steep, rocky slopes without falling. The ground doesn't get easier. The feet get surer. The book ends with a note for the choir leader about stringed instruments: this cry of faith from the edge of disaster was meant to be sung together. Some Christians turn to these verses in hard seasons, and some read Habakkuk as a pattern for honest prayer: complain first, wait on the watchtower, then sing. The yet doesn't cancel the complaint. It comes after it.

`FEET LIKE A DEER'S ON THE ROCKS.`
then, large: `YET I WILL REJOICE IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: If today is hard, let it be hard, and name what's not blooming, money, health, a relationship, plans that fell apart, plainly, the way Habakkuk listed his empty fields. Then look for one thing that's still good, a person who loves you, light through a window, a song you know by heart, and rest your attention there. If you pray, say Habakkuk's yet in your own heart; if not, let that one good thing be enough for now.
Hinds' feet. What Habakkuk says God gives him for climbing steep, rocky ground: not an easier path, but surer footing.
Your line: yet I will rejoice. The ground stays steep; the feet get surer. That's day four hundred ninety-one.

492.title: He will sing over you (Zephaniah 3:17)
492.hook: God will rejoice over you with singing
492.howItsDone: Some churches read Zephaniah 3:14–20 during Advent, and some Christians choose verse 17 for baptisms, weddings and blessings over children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hinds' feet: Habakkuk's sure steps on rocky ground, and his song from the edge. Your line: yet I will rejoice.

A parent at bedtime, the same song every night, slightly off key. A whole restaurant singing happy birthday while the guest of honor tries to hide under the table. A choir at a funeral. Being sung to is strange and tender. The one being sung to does nothing; they just receive it. In church, the singing mostly goes one way: people sing to God. Hymns, praise songs, chants. But tucked at the end of a short book full of warnings, the direction flips. There, it's God who sings.

The book is Zephaniah, three short chapters set in the days of King Josiah. Most of it is thunder: warnings of the day of the LORD, a day of wrath, darkness and alarm. A medieval Latin hymn about the last judgment, the Dies Irae, day of wrath, takes its opening words from Zephaniah's first chapter. So you'd expect the book to end in smoke. Instead, chapter three turns. Sing, daughter of Zion. Shout. Be glad. The judgment is lifted. Then this, in the King James Bible: "The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing." God isn't far off on a throne, but in the midst of thee, in the middle of the crowd, rejoicing over the people like a parent over a newborn, or a groom at a wedding. The middle phrase is a puzzle: he will rest in his love. The Hebrew can also be read as he will be silent in his love, or he will quiet you with his love. Translators differ. Maybe it's both: a love so deep it goes quiet, then breaks into song. Some Christians choose this verse for baptisms and weddings, and some families paint it on a nursery wall. The God of the day of wrath, the book says, is also the God who sings over you.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, near or far, or someone gone, and picture them resting, safe. Then, very quietly, hum any tune over them, a lullaby, a hymn, a song from the car radio; you don't need words, or to sing well. If you pray, hold them before God as you hum; if not, let the song carry your care.
Dies Irae. The medieval Latin hymn of judgment and wrath that borrows its opening words from Zephaniah, the same book that ends with God singing.
Your line: sung over. You don't have to do a thing to be sung to. Until tomorrow.

493.title: Consider your ways (Haggai 1:2–8)
493.hook: you eat but aren't full; you earn wages into a bag with holes
493.howItsDone: Some churches read Haggai when they are building or rebuilding, and some Christians use its call to consider your ways as a prompt for an honest review of how they spend their time and money.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dies Irae, and the surprise at the end of Zephaniah: God sings over you. Your line: sung over.

Payday. The money lands, and by the end of the week, somehow, it's gone. Not on anything big. Just leaking: groceries that didn't last, subscriptions you forgot, little fixes on things that keep breaking. Working hard and never quite getting ahead. An old prophet named Haggai described exactly that, with an image anyone who's carried coins can picture: a bag with holes in it. He wasn't talking to lazy people. He was talking to people who were busy, and tired, and couldn't figure out why it never felt like enough.

Haggai's first message is dated to the day: the second year of King Darius, the sixth month, the first day. The exiles have come home from Babylon to Jerusalem, and the temple is still a ruin. People say it isn't the right time to rebuild. Haggai's answer, in the King James Bible: "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?" Cieled means paneled, finished nicely, while God's house sits in rubble. Then: "Consider your ways." In Hebrew it's more vivid: set your heart on your ways. Look hard at where your life is going. Then the list: "Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes." Every line has the same shape: effort in, nothing to show for it. Haggai's diagnosis is that the people have put their own houses first and left the center empty. So the cure is surprisingly practical: go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build. Christians read Haggai more than one way. Some hear it about church buildings and giving. Others hear it more broadly: when the most important thing in a life is left in ruins, everything else leaks. And the people listened. Before the month was out, by Haggai's own dates, they started rebuilding.
screen: `DATED TO THE DAY: A TEMPLE IN RUINS.`

segments.voice: Picture your last week as a bag you've been filling with time, energy, money and attention, and find one hole: hours on a screen that left you emptier, or worry about something you can't change. Then ask Haggai's question: what's the thing at the center I've left in ruins? If you pray, set it before God and ask for one first step; if not, simply name it, and name the first piece of wood.
Cieled. The old word for paneled, finished nicely: the houses Haggai says the people built for themselves while God's house lay in ruins.
Your line: a bag with holes. The people listened, and started to build. Day four hundred ninety-three, done.

494.title: Not by might (Zechariah 4:6)
494.hook: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit
494.tomorrow: your king comes on a donkey
494.howItsDone: Some Christians quote Zechariah 4:6 when starting a work that feels too big, such as founding a church or a ministry, and some read the lampstand's oil as a picture of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cieled houses and Haggai's warning about wages that leak away. Your line: a bag with holes.

Same city, same year, same half-built temple as yesterday. Haggai told the people to build, and they did. The man in charge is Zerubbabel, the governor, a descendant of the old kings, with a small crew of returned exiles, not much money, hostile neighbors, and a foundation that looks like nothing next to the stories of Solomon's temple. Haggai himself asks who is left who saw the first house in its glory, and whether this one looks like nothing beside it. Into that discouragement steps a second prophet, Zechariah. He doesn't bring a budget. He brings a vision.

Zechariah sees a lampstand of solid gold with seven lamps, and on either side, two olive trees that seem to feed oil straight into the lamps. Nobody presses olives, hauls jars or refills anything. The light just keeps burning, fed from a source the lamps don't control. Zechariah asks the angel what it means. The answer, in the King James Bible: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts." The word for might can also mean an army, or wealth, or strength. Power is the strength of your own arm. Zerubbabel has neither, and God says that's fine. That's not how this gets built. Then a picture for the governor's problem: "Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain." The mountain might be the opposition, or the sheer size of the task. Either way, it flattens. When the last stone goes on, the people will shout grace, grace unto it. A few verses later comes a question: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" The little foundation that looked like nothing is not to be despised. Small beginnings count. Some Christians read the vision as a picture of the Holy Spirit, the oil that keeps the lamp burning. Others hear a word for any work that seems too big for the people doing it: churches, families, movements, one person trying to change. The work still needs hands; Zerubbabel still lays the stones. But the light isn't his to manufacture.

For a few breaths, loosen it: not quitting, since Zerubbabel kept building, just admitting the oil isn't yours to make. If you pray, hand that one thing to God's spirit; if not, simply let your hands open on your lap.
Zerubbabel. The governor with a small crew and a big job, told the mountain before him would become a plain, not by might but by God's spirit.
Your line: grace, grace unto it. Small beginnings count, even when they look like nothing. See you tomorrow.

495.title: Your king comes on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9)
495.hook: lowly and riding on a donkey: words the gospels saw on Palm Sunday
495.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday, the Sunday before Easter, many churches hold processions with palm branches and read the Gospel of Jesus entering Jerusalem on a donkey, often alongside Zechariah 9:9.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zerubbabel and the golden lampstand: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit. Your line: grace, grace unto it.

Leaders arrive with motorcades and flashing lights, or a jet on the tarmac. In the ancient world, a conquering king rode in on a warhorse or stood in a chariot, soldiers marching behind and captives in chains. The animal said everything: I won, and I can do it again. Now a different arrival: crowds, shouting, branches in the road, and at the center a man on a young donkey, his feet nearly scraping the ground. Many churches remember that scene every year on Palm Sunday. But the picture was painted centuries earlier, in the same book as yesterday's vision.

In the King James Bible: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass." Ass is the old English word for a donkey. Zechariah announces a king, the trumpets are ready, and then he says lowly. The Hebrew can also mean poor, or humbled: a king who is just and brings rescue, but comes without swagger. The next verse explains the donkey. God says the chariot and the warhorse will be cut off, the battle bow broken, and this king will speak peace to the nations. A donkey is the animal of farmers and traders, of ordinary days: a peace animal. The king arrives disarmed on purpose. Centuries later, the Gospels tell how Jesus sent two disciples to bring a donkey and rode it down the Mount of Olives into Jerusalem, as crowds spread cloaks and branches. Matthew and John both quote Zechariah to explain it. One curious detail: Zechariah, like much Hebrew poetry, says the same thing twice, an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass. Matthew's account has two animals, a donkey and her colt. Readers have discussed that for centuries. Jews still read Zechariah's king as a hope for the future; Christians hear it fulfilled on Palm Sunday. Either way the picture holds: power that chooses to come low.
screen: then, large: `LOWLY, AND RIDING UPON AN ASS.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where you hold some power, a parent, a boss, the one with the car keys, and picture a moment coming up where you could choose the donkey over the warhorse: ask instead of order, listen before deciding, let someone else go first. Lowly doesn't mean weak; Zechariah's king is still a king. If you pray, ask for that kind of strength; if not, picture yourself arriving gently.
Ani, Hebrew for lowly, poor or humbled: Zechariah's word for a just king arriving lowly, on the animal of peace, which the Gospels saw on Palm Sunday.
Your line: lowly, riding. A king, and still on a donkey. That's day four hundred ninety-five.

496.title: Turn the hearts (Malachi 4:5–6)
496.hook: the last lines of the Protestant Old Testament: hearts of parents turned to children
496.howItsDone: Some churches read Malachi in Advent, as the prophecy of a messenger before the Lord, and pair it with the Gospel stories of John the Baptist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ani: Zechariah's lowly king, riding a donkey instead of a warhorse. Your line: lowly, riding.

In a Protestant Bible, the Old Testament ends with Malachi. Turn the page, and the next thing is the first line of Matthew, a list of names. Between them sits a silence the Bible doesn't fill. So whatever Malachi says last stands right at the seam. You might expect a grand vision, or a thunderclap. Instead, the final words are about something small and close to home. Families. Parents and children. Who's speaking to whom, and who isn't.

Malachi's name means my messenger, and it may be a title rather than a name. His book is a series of arguments between God and the people, about tired worship, broken promises and marriages, and the poor being cheated. Then the end, in the King James Bible: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD: And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." Elijah doesn't die in 2 Kings; he's carried up in a whirlwind. So the hope grew that he'd come back, to prepare the way for God. At the Passover seder, Jewish tradition pours a cup for Elijah and opens the door for him. And look at Elijah's work: not defeating enemies, but mending families, turning hearts across the generations, both ways. Then the very last words warn that otherwise God will strike the land with a curse. That ending is so hard that in synagogue readings the verse before it is read again afterward, so the book closes on Elijah and hope. These words come back soon. In the opening chapter of Luke, an angel promises that a child named John will come in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. Christians read John the Baptist as the Elijah Malachi promised. So the Old Testament, in this arrangement, ends with a family reunion still waiting to happen.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone a generation away from you, a parent or a child, or if they're gone or far away, a grandparent, a niece, a mentor, and notice what's between you: warmth, distance, an old hurt, a thing unsaid. Don't try to fix it all; just let your heart turn toward them a few degrees, the way Malachi pictures it. If you pray, bring them before God by name; if not, simply hold them in mind with care.
Malachi, meaning my messenger: his last promise that Elijah would come and turn the hearts of parents to children, and children to parents.
Your line: open the door for Elijah. Hearts turn both ways, parents and children alike. Until tomorrow.

497.title: Wipe away tears (Isaiah 25:6–8)
497.hook: a feast of rich food for all peoples, and death swallowed up
497.howItsDone: Isaiah 25:6–9 is among the funeral readings in some churches, and some Christians connect its feast with the communion meal and with the hope of resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malachi, and Elijah sent to turn the hearts of parents and children. Your line: open the door for Elijah.

After a funeral, there's usually food. A long table in a church hall, casseroles under foil, someone's famous potato salad, coffee in big urns. People who haven't seen each other in years stand holding paper plates, and between the tears there's sometimes laughter. Grief and a meal, side by side. Today Isaiah takes that same table and turns it inside out: a feast where the guest list is everyone on earth, and what gets swallowed up at the end of the meal is death.
screen: `GRIEF AND A MEAL, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the menu, in the King James Bible: "a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined." Fat things meant the best food, the richest cuts. Wine on the lees is wine left to age on its sediment until it's deep and smooth. It's a banquet, set on God's mountain, for all people, every nation. Then the feast turns. God removes the covering cast over all peoples, the veil spread over all nations. Some readers hear a burial shroud, the cloth laid over the dead, lifted off the whole human race. And then: "He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." Some readers hear an echo of older stories from that region, where death was a swallower with a huge mouth. Here, the swallower gets swallowed. After the victory, God doesn't make a speech. God goes face to face, wiping tears off cheeks one by one, like a parent after a nightmare. The New Testament picks these words up twice. Paul quotes the swallowing of death when he writes about the resurrection. And near the very end of the Bible, Revelation says: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." Christians hear in this feast a picture of what they hope for. This week's prophets walked us here: Habakkuk's yet, the God who sings, a bag with holes, Zerubbabel, the donkey king, hearts turned. And now, a table set for everyone.
screen: then, large: `HE WILL SWALLOW UP DEATH IN VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, or someone grieving now, and let yourself feel it for a moment; Isaiah's feast doesn't skip the tears. Then picture a table and who you'd want at it, someone lonely, someone far from home, and picture setting the plate in front of them. If you pray, give thanks for the people at your table; if not, simply hold them in mind.
Shroud, the burial cloth laid over the dead: Isaiah's picture of God lifting it off every nation at a feast where death is swallowed up.
Your line: tears wiped away. Face by face, one by one. Day four hundred ninety-seven, and another week walked.
